en: It has been stated that Brahman, the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, is that which is to be known through the Vedāntas;
however, that is incorrect, for it is not something to be established by a [single] sentence.
Anticipating the objection that [the Lord] is established by means of inference, he says:
"Because He has the scripture as His source" (Śāstrayonitvāt). 1.1.3.
That whose source, cause, or authority is the scripture (śāstra) is "śāstrayoni."

Its state is "having the scripture as its source" (*śāstrayonitva*); therefore, because the scripture is the cause of the knowledge of Brahman, Brahman has that as its source. Since Brahman, being entirely beyond the senses, is not an object of perception and other means of valid cognition, and thus has the scripture alone as its means of valid cognition, the sentence beginning with "from which indeed these beings [arise]" makes known Brahman whose nature has been described.
The meaning is "indeed."
But is it not the case that Brahman cannot have the scripture as its source,
because Brahman is knowable through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
whereas scripture is purposeful only with regard to what is not already established?
What, then, is the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) regarding that?
It is not, first of all, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
For that is of two kinds: arising from the sense faculties (*indriya-sambhava*) and arising from yoga (*yoga-sambhava*).
Furthermore, it is twofold: arising from the sense faculties (*indriya-saṃbhava*) and arising from what is internal (*antar-saṃbhava*).

External sense faculties produce cognitions of their own objects that are capable of contact with what is present; thus, they do not produce cognitions of a specific person who is capable of directly perceiving all objects or of creating them. Nor [do they produce such cognitions] internally.
For it is impossible for that [cognition] to function with respect to external objects—distinct from internal pleasure, pain, and so forth—without depending upon the external sense organs.
Nor is it produced by yoga;

for although that which arises at the culmination of the intensification of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) possesses vivid manifestation, it lacks validity because it is merely a memory of an object previously experienced. Thus, how can it be considered perception?
Because there is no reason for it to have an object other than that [already perceived]; if that were the case, it would possess the nature of an error.
Nor is it inference, specifically that which is based on what has been previously observed (*viśeṣatodṛṣṭa*).
Or it may be *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on general observation).
Because there is an absence of the determination of a relationship with respect to an object beyond the senses (*atīndriya*), it cannot be *viśeṣatodṛṣṭa* (inference based on specific observation).
Even *sāmānyatodṛṣṭa* does not provide a valid mark (*liṅga*) that is restricted to a particular person capable of directly perceiving all things and creating them.
But is it not the case that the world’s status as an effect is pervaded by having a creator who is cognizant of its material cause, instruments, recipient, and purpose?
Furthermore, the world, being composed of non-conscious matter, is pervaded by dependence on a single conscious being;
for every effect, such as a jar, is observed to have a creator who is cognizant of its material cause, instruments, recipient, and purpose.
One's own body is insentiently originated, free from disease, and dependent on a single sentient being.
Furthermore, the world is an effect because it possesses constituent parts; this is what is stated. Now, what is this "dependence on a single sentient being"?
It is not, first of all, that their arising and subsistence are dependent upon him; for the illustrative example would then be deficient in the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*),
since one's own healthy body does not have its arising and subsistence dependent on a single conscious agent.
This is because the production and maintenance of that body, as well as all sentient beings such as wives and others who are its experiencers, are produced by *adṛṣṭa* (unseen merit/demerit).
Furthermore, the maintenance of a whole body in the form of inherence in its own parts does not depend upon a conscious being apart from the conjunction of those parts.

However, maintenance characterized by vital breath (*prāṇana*) is not possible in the earth, oceans, and mountains, which are intended as the subject of the argument (*pakṣa*). Thus, we do not perceive a single uniform type of maintenance that is common to both the subject and the similar instances (*sapakṣa*).

If it is argued that "dependence upon that" means "subordination to that," there is a deviation [from the rule] in the case of heavy chariots, boulders, trees, and so forth, which are accomplished by many conscious agents.
If it means "subordination to consciousness in general," then you are proving what is already established (*siddhasādhyatā*).
Furthermore, it is more reasonable to accept agency for the individual souls (*jīvas*) alone, as they are established by both disputants;
nor is agency impossible for souls due to their lack of knowledge regarding material causes and so forth,
because all conscious beings possess the capacity to directly perceive material causes such as earth and the like, as well as the instruments such as sacrifices.

Just as the earth and so forth, as well as sacrifices and the like, are perceived directly at present, there is no impossibility of sentient beings being agents even in the absence of direct perception of the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)— denoted by terms such as *apūrva*— which consists of the capacity inherent in the sacrifices and other means; for the commencement of an effect does not depend upon the direct perception of that [unseen force].
For it is the direct realization of one who possesses devotion that is useful for the commencement of an action;
however, in the case of power (*śakti*), mere knowledge alone is required,
not direct realization.

For potters and the like do not begin the production of effects such as jars or water-jars only after directly perceiving their causal capacity, just as they perceive the staff, the wheel, and other implements that serve as the means for the effect.
However, in this case, it is not untenable for conscious beings— who possess specific powers regarding sacrifices and so forth known through scripture— to initiate an action.
Furthermore, it is observed that only that which is possible to produce and whose materials and so forth can be known is seen to have an intelligent agent as its creator.
However, the earth, mountains, great oceans, and so forth, being impossible to produce and impossible to know their materials and so forth, do not have an intelligent creator.

Therefore, the quality of being an effect (*kāryatva*) residing only in things like jars and pots—which belong to the same class as those things that are possible to produce and whose materials and so forth can be known—is capable of proving that they are preceded by an intelligent creator.

Furthermore, since effects such as jars are seen to be created by one who is not the Lord (anīśvara), possesses limited knowledge and power, is embodied, subject to grasping, and has unfulfilled desires, this reason of "being an effect" (kāryatva) would be contradictory (viruddha) because it establishes a conscious agent who is the opposite of the desired [subject's] omniscience, omnipotence, and so forth.
Nor does this entail the undesirable consequence of the total abolition of all inference.

When the subject possessing the mark (*liṅgin*) is within the scope of another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), those contrary particulars established by the force of the mark recede, their movement being obstructed by that other means of valid cognition.

But here, with respect to the subject possessing the mark—which is beyond the range of all other means of valid cognition and is skilled in every kind of creation—all properties whose necessity of invariable concomitance has been understood through positive and negative instances would apply without distinction.
Because there is no subverting means of valid cognition (*nivartakapramāṇa*), things remain exactly as they are.
Therefore, how can God (*īśvara*) be established without scripture (*āgama*)?
To this, they reply: since the world possesses parts, its status as an effect (*kāryatva*) cannot be denied.
And there are formal arguments (prayoga): "The earth, mountains, and so forth, which are the subject of dispute, are effects, because they possess parts,
like a jar and other such things."
Likewise, that which is the subject of dispute— the earth, oceans, mountains, and so forth—
is an effect, because, while possessing magnitude, it possesses activity, like a jar. The body, the world, and so forth are effects.
"Because it possesses magnitude and is corporeal,
like a jar. Among substances that possess parts, we do not perceive any other characteristic besides having parts that serves as the regulator for why this [effect] is produced and not another.
If it is argued that "the state of being capable of being produced and the knowledge of the possible materials and so forth are perceived as restricted to the nature of being an effect," we say no.

Even when an object is inferred to be an effect, the capacity for knowledge regarding it is itself to be inferred from that effect; thus, in other cases as well, once the nature of being an effect is known through the presence of parts and so forth, those two [capacities] are already established. There is no distinction here.

For instance, when jars, water-pots, and the like have been made, a person who possesses the knowledge of the creator’s capacity to fashion them—having inferred that capacity from the observation of the effects—[perceives] something never seen before.

Having observed the palace of a king with its various architectural arrangements, and having ascertained its status as an effect (*kāryatva*) by means of the specific configuration of its constituent parts, one immediately infers the diversity of the creator's knowledge and power.

Thus, once the fact that the body, the world, and so forth are effects is established, a particular person who is skilled in the direct perception of all things and in their creation is indeed proven to exist.

Furthermore, even though the experience of pleasure and pain by all sentient beings is caused by merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*), [this would not be possible] if they were not presided over by a conscious being.

Since it is impossible for those two [space and time], being insentient, to function as cause and effect, one must postulate someone who is capable of bestowing all fruits in accordance with all karmas; for we do not observe that an insentient tool such as an axe, when not presided over by a carpenter, serves as a means for constructing a sacrificial post (yūpa) even when many auxiliary factors like place and time are present. To raise the objection of deviation (*vyabhicāra*) on the grounds of seeds and sprouts—which are included within the very category under discussion—is merely the manifestation of ignorance on the part of these "Vedic scholars" who are like zombies.
The statement regarding the deviation [of the reason] by means of pleasure and so forth is likewise [invalid].
Furthermore, it is not reasonable to postulate that the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls), who are accepted by both disputants, are the such controllers on the grounds of parsimony (*lāghava*);
for their capacity to perceive the subtle, the concealed, and the remote has been ascertained.
For everywhere, conceptual construction conforms to what is perceived;
and there is no certainty regarding the Lord’s incapacity, as there is in the case of the individual soul (*kṣetrajña*).
Therefore, it is not impossible for His existence to be established through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

Established by the reason that an effect is necessarily preceded by a capable agent, [the subject] is established as being endowed precisely with natural omniscience and the power to govern it. As for the objection raised— that this proves the opposite of the specific attributes [of the deity] by implying a lack of sovereignty and so forth— [it is refuted as follows]:
This is based on ignorance regarding the operation of inference;

for it is impossible to establish, in the subject of inference (*liṅgin*), all those properties that are observed together in the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), including those that are not causes of the effect.
This is what is meant:
When something is being produced by someone for its own arising, it requires that agent’s capacity for its own creation and knowledge of its own material causes and instruments;
however, it does not require the incapacity of others or the knowledge of others, because those lack the status of being causes.

Since its own production is established solely through the capacity for self-emanation and the knowledge of its own material cause (upādāna) and instruments (upakaraṇa), it is illogical to postulate that something else— such as the cognition of another object— which is irrelevant to the process and merely appears as a correlate, can serve as its cause. Thus,
[the cognition] does not first of all have everything as its object.
For a potter or the like does not fail to know anything other than what is being made, nor is their knowledge restricted to only a few objects;
for among all agents, there is no fixed rule regarding ignorance or incapacity with respect to this or that thing, as such ignorance and so forth vary across all individuals. Therefore:

Since the non-establishment of [qualities] such as non-omnipotence—which do not prove the fact of being an effect—does not lead to the cognition of those qualities in the subject (liṅgin), there is no fallacy of proving the opposite.

If it is argued that since the superintendence of potters and others over their tools, such as the staff and the wheel, is observed only by means of a body, it is therefore impossible for a bodiless Lord to superintend the material causes and instruments of the world, we say no;
for we observe the removal, destruction, or neutralization of spirits, poisons, and the like residing in another's body through mere volition alone.
If it is asked how there can be a volition, which consists in the impelling of another, for one who is bodiless; [the answer is:
volition does not depend upon a body, because the body lacks the status of being a cause of volition.
For the mind alone is the cause of volition (saṃkalpa);
this is accepted even in the case of the Lord (īśvara),
since, by virtue of being an effect, the mind is established as possessing the power of cognition just like [the Lord's] knowledge.
If it is argued that mental volition belongs only to one who possesses a body, because only one with a body possesses a mind, we say no;
for since the mind is eternal, its existence persists even upon the departure of the body, and thus the reason is inconclusive.

Therefore, since the *kṣetrajña*— being subject to merit and demerit and possessing limited power and knowledge— is not capable of fashioning effects such as bodies and worlds with their various specific arrangements of parts, there must exist a distinct Person (*puruṣaviśeṣa*) who is skilled in the creation of the entire universe, possessed of inconceivable, immeasurable knowledge, power, and sovereignty, bodiless, and whose infinite, vast, and variegated manifold of manifestations is accomplished solely through the means of His mere volition.
The Lord is established by inference alone;
therefore, because Brahman is to be understood through another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), this sentence does not establish Brahman.

Furthermore, since it is observed that only two things that are absolutely distinct—such as clay and a potter—can respectively function as material cause (*upādāna*) and instrumental cause (*nimitta*), [it follows that] for space and so forth...
Furthermore, because it is impossible for a partless substance to be an effect, one cannot maintain that Brahman alone is both the efficient cause and the material cause of the entire universe.
This being the case, we reply: the statement concerning the origin and so forth (*janmādivākya*) indeed makes known Brahman as defined by the aforementioned characteristics.
Why? Because Brahman has scripture alone as its means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
As for what was said—that the entire world is an effect because it possesses parts and so forth—[that is not so].

It is observed that an effect is preceded by a specific agent capable of producing it; therefore, someone who is skilled in knowing the creation of the entire world, as well as its material causes and instruments, must be inferred.
This is incorrect, because even if the earth, the great oceans, and so forth are effects, there is no evidence that they were created all at once by a single being.
Furthermore, all things do not share a single commonality of being effects in the same way as a single jar, such that there would be a single creator for them all at once;
for when effects are distinct, we observe differences in both time and agent, and thus no rule of identity regarding agent and time is observed.

Nor can it be argued that because the individual knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) possess the power to create a diverse world, and because this must be inferred as an effect, one must postulate a creator distinct from them; for such a multiplicity of postulations is untenable.

This is because we observe a variety of powers even among the *kṣetrajñas* themselves who have accumulated specific merits, and since it is possible for those very individuals—through the presence of extraordinary unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*)—to be the causes of their respective distinct effects.
For it is illogical to postulate a person who is distinct from these and absolutely unobserved;
furthermore, neither the simultaneous arising of all things nor the simultaneous destruction of all things enters the path of valid cognition, because such is never observed,
and because arising and destruction are seen to occur only in succession.
Furthermore, when the production and destruction of all things are postulated as being effects, there is no contradiction in making such a postulation in accordance with what is observed.
Therefore, when "having a single intelligent creator" is the property to be proven (*sādhya*), the reason (*hetu*) of "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is inconclusive (*anaikāntika*),
and the subject (*pakṣa*) suffers from the fallacy of having an unestablished qualification (*aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva*).
Furthermore, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*),

because a single being who is skilled in all emanations is not established. If the probandum is merely "having an intelligent creator," it results in proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatā*).
Does this "effectness" (*kāryatva*), which is intended to prove the existence of some single being endowed with omniscience and omnipotence, pertain to all things produced simultaneously?
Or does it pertain to all things produced successively?
If it pertains to all things produced simultaneously, then the property of "effectness" is unestablished (*asiddha*).
If [the argument] were to apply to all things arising sequentially, it would be contradictory because it would prove that they have multiple agents.
Furthermore, in proving a single agent for this [Veda] as well, there is contradiction with perception and inference, as well as contradiction with scripture.
This is because of scriptural statements such as "a potter is born" and "a chariot-maker is born.

Furthermore, since all effects— including bodies and the like— are observed to be permeated by pleasure and so forth, which are themselves effects of the qualities such as *sattva*, it must necessarily be admitted that they have *sattva* and the other qualities as their root cause.
The specific qualities (viśeṣas) residing in the cause, such as *sattva* and the others, are the causes of the diversity of effects.
The production of those effects from that [cause] occurs by way of the modifications of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) associated with the Puruṣa who possesses them.

And the Puruṣa’s connection with them is rooted in karma. Therefore, for the sake of initiating specific effects, the agent’s connection with karma must necessarily be accepted as a cause of the effect, just like the power of knowledge (*jñānaśakti*).
Furthermore, since the diversity of the power of knowledge is rooted in karma,

even though desire is the cause for the commencement of an action, because that desire— when qualified by a specific object— is rooted in the existence [of past impressions], its connection with karma is unavoidable. Therefore, the individual souls (kṣetrajñas) alone are the agents.
Nothing distinct from that [world] is established by inference.
Furthermore, there are formal arguments (prayoga): "The body, the world, and so forth, have a conscious being (kṣetrajña) as their agent, because they are effects, like a jar."
The Lord is not an agent,
because he lacks a purpose,
like a liberated soul.
The Lord is not an agent because he is bodiless, just like that [other disembodied being].
Nor is there any deviation [from this rule] in the case of the individual souls (kṣetrajña) regarding their presiding over their own bodies.
Even there, because of the existence of the subtle body of the beginningless [self],
time is not an object of dispute as being devoid of the world,
since it possesses the nature of time.
"As in the case of the present time.
Furthermore, does God perform his work while possessing a body or without a body?
First of all, he does not do so without a body.
Because agency is not observed in that which is bodiless;
even mental effects belong only to one who possesses a body,
for although the mind is eternal, its effects are not seen in liberated beings who are bodiless.
Nor is he possessed of a body, because that [position] cannot withstand analysis: is that body eternal or non-eternal?
It cannot first be eternal;
If that [body] were composed of parts and eternal, there would be no contradiction in the world also being eternal, which would result in the non-establishment of God.
Nor is it non-eternal;
for at that time, there is an absence of any cause for its body other than itself.
If it is argued that he himself is the cause, we say no; for that is impossible for one who is bodiless.
If it is argued that he possesses a body by means of another body, we say no.
Because it would lead to an infinite regress. Is it active or inactive?
Precisely because it is bodiless, it is not active.
Nor does that which is devoid of activity produce an effect, like a liberated soul.
If it is asserted that the world, as an effect, has the activity of mere will as its agent, then the subject (pakṣa) possesses an unestablished qualification (aprasiddhaviśeṣaṇatva),
and the example (dṛṣṭānta) lacks the property to be proven (sādhyahīnatā).

Therefore, since inference regarding Īśvara based on conformity with perception is itself contradicted by that very conformity, the Supreme Lord—the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman—is known solely through the authority of the Śāstra. For the Śāstra establishes Him as an ocean of infinite, unsurpassed, immeasurable, and noble qualities—such as omniscience and the realization of true volitions—which are entirely dissimilar to all things perceived by other means of knowledge, and whose nature is the absolute opposite of everything that is to be rejected. Consequently, there is no possibility of even a trace of the defects associated with objects determined through other means of knowledge.

As for the objection that the identity of the efficient cause and the material cause is unobserved— and that the fact that a partless substance such as space (*ākāśa*) is an effect is impossible to establish—

that too is not contradictory; this will be demonstrated in the sections "The Source [is Brahman], because there is no contradiction with the proposition and the illustrative examples" and "Space does not [originate], because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect]."

Therefore, since it is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition and is thus the exclusive object of scripture, it is established that the sentence "from which indeed these beings [are born]" teaches Brahman as defined above. 1.1.3.
